sentences.text: The genus Machairoceratops contains only one known species, M. cronusi, which is known solely from the holotype specimen UMNH VP 20550. This four-legged herbivore possessed a frill to protect its neck, a common feature among ceratopsids.

Its genus name means "bent sword" because of the two forward-curving horns located at the top of its frill. The species name cronusi honors the Greek god Cronus, who is depicted in mythology carrying a curved sickle. The top of its skull featured a single pair of long, curved spikes that were 44 centimeters long.
Unlike other centrosaurines, the sides of its frill lacked smaller epiparietal bones. Its postorbital horns measured 27 centimeters in length, though their exact orientation on the skull is unknown.
The holotype specimen is approximately the same size as the dinosaur Diabloceratops.
It belongs to the family Ceratopsidae. It is classified within the subfamily Centrosaurinae.

Researchers tested its position within the subfamily Centrosaurinae using maximum parsimony and Bayesian phylogenetic analyses. The maximum parsimony analysis resulted in a large polytomy at the base of Centrosaurinae, resolving only specific subgroups like Centrosaurini and a clade of Avaceratops and Nasutoceratops. In contrast, the Bayesian analysis produced a fully resolved evolutionary tree.

This extinct centrosaurine dinosaur lived during the Late Cretaceous in the Wahweap Formation of southern Utah, United States. It lived during the Late Cretaceous, between 80 and 77 million years ago, in what is now North America.

The precise age of the animal is estimated to be 80.06 million years ago, with an uncertainty range between 80.68 and 79.26 million years ago. The genus time range is recorded as Campanian to Campanian, spanning from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.

When it lived, the Western Interior Seaway was at its widest, nearly isolating southern Laramidia from the rest of North America. Its habitat included lakes, floodplains, and rivers flowing to the east. Evidence suggests the climate was wet and seasonal.

There is ongoing debate regarding the evolutionary placement of Machairoceratops. While maximum parsimony analysis resulted in a large polytomy at the base of Centrosaurinae, resolving only specific subgroups, the Bayesian analysis produced a fully resolved evolutionary tree, suggesting different interpretations of its ancestry.
